notes: Ground truth for review-performance. Focused on patterns the source clearly exhibits: hot-loop allocations, unbounded buffers, sequential awaits in I/O-bounded code, redundant work on every render/tick. Static review only — no profiling fixtures.

findings.summary: sessionLog array grows unbounded with TX/RX log entries during a connected session; both the main-process Array and every renderer subscriber's mirror grow forever. Eventually triggers GC pressure and IPC backpressure.
findings.evidence: let sessionLog: LogEntry[] = []; addLog pushes without trimming. Every command logs at least TX and RX entries; the poll loop runs continuously.
findings.recommendation: Apply a ring-buffer cap in addLog (e.g. 10_000 entries, drop oldest). Mirror the cap in the renderer's log store.

findings.summary: Every serial RX chunk allocates two intermediate strings (`ascii` + `display` via two .replace() calls) and an addLog object for the log path. At ~20–50 chunks/sec under polling, this is sustained allocation churn.
findings.evidence: port.on('data', chunk => { const ascii = chunk.toString('ascii'); const display = ascii.replace(/\r/g, '\\r').replace(/\n/g, '\\n'); addLog({...}); elm?.onData(ascii); });
findings.recommendation: Move the display escape into a debug-only path gated by a verbose flag, or batch chunks for a single log entry per command response. The hot path should just forward ascii to elm.onData.

findings.summary: discoverSupportedPIDs() awaits each of the 4 support-range requests sequentially even though they're independent ELM commands. Since ELM is single-command serial, this is forced — but the 3000ms timeout per range means a non-responsive ECM stalls discovery for 12s.
findings.evidence: for (const rangePID of supportRanges) { const resp = await this.elm.send(rangePID, 3000); ... } — 4 ranges × 3s = 12s worst case.
findings.recommendation: Shorten the per-range timeout to 1500ms (ELM auto-timing handles longer responses), and break out early once a range returns NO DATA (subsequent ranges depend on prior bitmask bits indicating support).

findings.summary: formatContext is called fresh on every claude:ask, rebuilding the entire snapshot string by Array.push + join even when only the question changed. With the current chat UI sending the full snapshot per turn, this is wasted work and bloats the input tokens (no prompt-caching boundary placed).
findings.evidence:
askClaude builds messages with `<session-snapshot>
${formatContext(ctx)}
</session-snapshot>

${question}` inside the user content block, mixing stable context with the volatile question. The Anthropic SDK supports `cache_control: {type: 'ephemeral'}` at message boundaries.
findings.recommendation: Split the user message into two content blocks: a stable `<session-snapshot>...</session-snapshot>` block with `cache_control: {type: 'ephemeral'}`, then the question. Saves input tokens on every follow-up turn in the same chat.

findings.summary: pollSinglePID allocates a new PIDReading object every poll. At 10–20 Hz across 15 PIDs, this is ~150–300 small object allocations per second. Acceptable on desktop but worth tightening if the renderer chokes.
findings.evidence: const reading: PIDReading = { pid, value, raw: bytes, timestamp: Date.now(), unit: definition.unit }; emit('pid-reading', reading) — allocated even when value didn't change since last poll.
findings.recommendation: Reuse a per-PID PIDReading object and mutate fields, OR add a `value === lastValue` short-circuit before emitting (saves both allocation and IPC traffic).

findings.summary: onData does `recvBuf += chunk` then a substring scan for '>' on every chunk. With incremental chunks from Bluetooth (often 1–4 bytes), this is O(n) per byte = O(n²) over a full response.
findings.evidence: onData() concatenates and re-checks the full recvBuf for ELM_PROMPT each chunk. For a 200-byte response delivered in 50 BT chunks, that's 50 × ~200 = 10000 char-checks.
findings.recommendation: Track the last-scanned offset and only search the newly-appended slice for the '>' prompt: `if (chunk.includes('>')) { ... }` plus a length-only update otherwise.

findings.summary: updatePIDReading rebuilds the entire liveData and history maps on every reading, triggering a full subscriber re-render even when the value didn't change.
findings.evidence: appStore.ts:updatePIDReading constructs new objects/maps per update; no value-changed short-circuit; subscribers re-render on identity change.
findings.recommendation: Short-circuit on value === previous in the action, and use shallow-merge per-PID (set state.liveData[pid] = reading) so unrelated subscribers don't re-render.

findings.summary: App root subscribes to the entire liveData object, so any single PID reading re-renders the root and recomputes derived counts.
findings.evidence: App.tsx selects the full liveData state and computes livePIDCount inline on every render.
findings.recommendation: Use a selector (`state => Object.keys(state.liveData).length`) and shallow-equal compare; or memoize the count derivation with `useMemo` keyed by the size.

findings.summary: liveCount runs PID_CATALOG.filter on every render of AllPIDsScreen without memoization.
findings.evidence: AllPIDsScreen.tsx:~162 — PID_CATALOG.filter(...) called inline in render body.
findings.recommendation: Wrap in `useMemo(() => PID_CATALOG.filter(...), [liveData])` keyed on the relevant slice.

scoring.method: Same scorer with category aliases tuned for performance.
